# Chronos Studio — Glossary

**242 terms**, grouped by topic and listed alphabetically within each group. The same definitions power the in-app tooltips: both are generated by `scripts/generate_glossary.py` from a single source, so they cannot disagree.

Definitions are deliberately short and in plain English. For the exact test, implementation and assumption behind each number, see [METHODS.md](METHODS.md).

## Contents

- [Basics](#basics) — 29 terms
- [Data & quality](#data--quality) — 19 terms
- [Stationarity & tests](#stationarity--tests) — 25 terms
- [Decomposition & components](#decomposition--components) — 18 terms
- [Correlation & model identification](#correlation--model-identification) — 12 terms
- [Models](#models) — 47 terms
- [Forecasting](#forecasting) — 14 terms
- [Evaluation](#evaluation) — 24 terms

## Basics

**Confidence level** (`confidence_level`) — The nominal long-run coverage of an interval procedure, e.g. 95%. It describes the method, not a probability for this one interval.

**Deterministic** (`deterministic`) — Containing no random component: the same inputs always give the same output. Narratives and advisor rules in this app are deterministic.

**Effect size** (`effect_size`) — The magnitude of an estimated effect, independent of sample size. Recommending a transform requires an effect, not just a small p-value.

**Ergodicity** (`ergodicity`) — The property that time averages converge to the ensemble average. It is what makes a single historical path enough to estimate a model.

**Estimate** (`estimate`) — A computed value of a parameter or quantity. Every number displayed is an estimate with a stated method, not a typed-in fact.

**Frequency** (`frequency`) — How often observations are recorded — daily, monthly, quarterly. The app infers it and never compares models fitted at different effective frequencies.

**Hypothesis test** (`hypothesis_test`) — A procedure that compares a statistic against a null distribution and returns a p-value. It never proves the null; it can only fail to reject it.

**Innovation** (`innovation`) — The one-step-ahead surprise, i.e. the residual after the model's conditional prediction. Residual diagnostics examine innovations, not fitted values.

**Lag** (`lag`) — A past value or a past error; lag k means k time steps back.

**Lead** (`lead`) — A future value. Forecasts are leads; leakage occurs when a lead influences a modelling choice.

**Level** (`level`) — The current underlying height of the series once short-term noise is smoothed out.

**Noise** (`noise`) — The irregular remainder left after trend, season and cycle are removed. It should look unstructured; structure here is a finding for the modelling stage.

**Observation** (`observation`) — One recorded value at one point in time. The count of observations is written n and is always shown beside any accuracy number.

**P value** (`p_value`) — The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of seeing a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. Small values are evidence against the null.

**Parameter** (`parameter`) — A number estimated from data inside a model, e.g. an AR coefficient. Its count enters AIC, BIC and AICc.

**Parametric** (`parametric`) — Assuming a finite, named distribution (e.g. Gaussian errors). Non-parametric or distribution-free methods avoid that assumption.

**Period** (`period`) — The number of observations in one full seasonal cycle, e.g. 12 for monthly data with a yearly pattern.

**Population** (`population`) — The hypothetical full data-generating process. Estimates describe the sample; intervals express uncertainty about the population.

**Random walk** (`random_walk`) — A series whose next value is the last value plus a shock. It has a unit root and its naive forecast is optimal.

**Robust** (`robust`) — Insensitive to a few unusual observations. Robust STL and median-based slopes are preferred where spikes are common.

**Sample** (`sample`) — The observed window used to estimate a model. It is split into training and test blocks, never interleaved.

**Season** (`season`) — The position within a cycle (January, Monday, hour 09). Distinct from seasonality, which is the repeating pattern itself.

**Seed** (`seed`) — An integer that fixes every random draw — simulation paths, bootstrap bands, ML splits — so a study can be reproduced exactly.

**Significance** (`significance`) — A pre-agreed threshold (usually 5%) at which a test is said to reject. The app prints the exact p-value so a reader can use their own threshold.

**Stationarity** (`stationarity`) — A series is stationary when its level, spread and dependence structure do not drift over time. Most classical models assume it, so we usually stabilise the series first.

**Stochastic process** (`stochastic_process`) — A collection of random variables indexed by time; a time series is one realised path from such a process.

**Time series** (`time_series`) — A sequence of observations indexed in time order, usually at a fixed frequency. Order is the information: shuffling the rows destroys the analysis.

**Trend** (`trend`) — The slow, long-run movement in the level of a series. It need not be linear and is estimated, not assumed away.

**White noise** (`white_noise`) — Uncorrelated, zero-mean, constant-variance shocks. A white-noise series has nothing to forecast; the app can return a 'no model needed' verdict.

## Data & quality

**Calendar heatmap** (`calendar_heatmap`) — A plot of values by calendar position (day × week/month) that makes missing days and weekly patterns visible.

**Column mapping** (`column_mapping`) — The user's declaration of which column is time, which is the value, and which are exogenous. Nothing is guessed silently.

**Constant run** (`constant_run`) — A stretch of identical values. Long runs can mean a stalled sensor rather than genuine stability.

**Content hash** (`content_hash`) — A fingerprint of the loaded values. Reports and archives carry it so a reader can prove which data produced a number.

**Data class** (`data_class`) — The branch chosen from the values themselves: continuous, count, intermittent, or event-timestamp. It decides which model families and metrics are legal.

**Dayfirst** (`dayfirst`) — Whether an ambiguous date like 03/04/2020 means 3 April (true) or 4 March (false). Stored in the column mapping.

**Duplicate timestamp** (`duplicate_timestamp`) — Two rows with the same time index. The app reports them and never silently drops a row.

**Gap** (`gap`) — A run of consecutive missing values. Short, medium and long gaps get different advice rather than one blanket imputation.

**Impossible value** (`impossible_value`) — A value that cannot occur (negative counts, a date outside the file's range). Flagged for review, never quietly deleted.

**Ingestion** (`ingestion`) — Reading CSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet, Stata or SPSS into a dated series with an explicit column mapping.

**Level shift** (`level_shift`) — A permanent step change in level. It is invisible in an STL remainder because STL absorbs it into the trend, so the app tests the deseasonalised series.

**Missing value** (`missing_value`) — A gap in the recorded series. Gaps are counted, reported and imputed only with an explicit, previewable operation.

**Outlier** (`outlier`) — An observation far from what its neighbours and season predict. The app flags spikes, level shifts and temporary changes separately.

**Overdispersion** (`overdispersion`) — Variance larger than the mean in count data. A mandatory pre-check before fitting Poisson, because it changes the whole likelihood.

**Provenance** (`provenance`) — The record of which stage, method and data version produced a result. Every recommendation is traceable to a displayed statistic.

**Resolution** (`resolution`) — The smallest step at which values are recorded, e.g. 0.1. It prevents an outlier rule from flagging rounding artefacts.

**Row order is time** (`row_order_is_time`) — The convention that physical row order defines time when no date column exists. It is recorded explicitly so it can be audited.

**Temporary change** (`temporary_change`) — A spike that decays back to the previous level. Unlike a level shift, it should not be modelled as a step dummy.

**Zero inflation** (`zero_inflation`) — More zeros than a standard count distribution predicts. It triggers zero-inflated or hurdle models and a metric-policy switch.

## Stationarity & tests

**ADF** (`adf`) — Augmented Dickey–Fuller test. Null: a unit root. Lags are chosen by AIC and MacKinnon p-values are used; three deterministic specifications are reported.

**ARCH-LM** (`arch_lm`) — Engle's Lagrange-multiplier test for autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity in residuals.

**Bai perron** (`bai_perron`) — A procedure for estimating several unknown break dates simultaneously with confidence intervals.

**Canova–Hansen** (`canova_hansen`) — A test of seasonal stability; rejection indicates seasonal unit roots that need seasonal differencing.

**Chow test** (`chow_test`) — An F-test for a break at a known, user-specified date.

**Cox stuart** (`cox_stuart`) — A sign test comparing the second half of a series with the first; catches slow drift without reacting to one jump.

**Cusum** (`cusum`) — A cumulative-sum test on recursive residuals for slow parameter drift.

**DF-GLS** (`df_gls`) — DF-GLS: a GLS-detrended Dickey–Fuller test with better small-sample power than ordinary ADF.

**Difference** (`difference`) — Replacing each value with the change from the previous one. Removes a trend; applying it to an already stable series adds noise and breaks the model.

**HEGY** (`hegy`) — Hylleberg–Engle–Granger–Yoo test that separates unit roots at the zero frequency from those at each seasonal frequency.

**Heteroskedasticity** (`heteroskedasticity`) — Variance that changes over time. ARCH-LM on the remainder detects it and points to a log/Box–Cox transform or a GARCH model.

**Integration order** (`integration_order`) — The number of differences needed for stationarity, written d in ARIMA(p,d,q). The app refuses more than two without a recorded justification.

**KPSS** (`kpss`) — Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin test. Null: stationarity. It is the mirror image of ADF, which is why the app reconciles the two rather than quoting one.

**MacKinnon p-values** (`mackinnon_p`) — Response-surface p-values for Dickey–Fuller statistics, used because the null distribution is non-standard.

**Mann kendall** (`mann_kendall`) — A distribution-free rank test for monotone trend. The app runs it on the deseasonalised series, not on a loess-smoothed trend.

**Normality battery** (`normality_battery`) — Shapiro–Wilk, Jarque–Bera and D'Agostino–Pearson applied together, because each is sensitive to a different departure.

**OCSB / CH** (`ocsb`) — Osborn–Chui–Smith–Birchenhall test for seasonal unit roots, used with HEGY and Canova–Hansen in the seasonal branch.

**Phillips–Perron** (`phillips_perron`) — A unit-root test that corrects the ADF statistic non-parametrically for serial correlation and heteroskedasticity instead of adding lags.

**Quandt andrews** (`quandt_andrews`) — A Chow test maximised over all candidate break dates, with a supremum statistic rather than a known breakpoint.

**Reconciliation** (`reconciliation`) — The 2×2 rule combining a unit-root test and a stationarity test into one verdict: both stationary, both non-stationary, or a contradiction needing judgement.

**Seasonal difference** (`seasonal_difference`) — Subtracting the value one full season ago. It removes a seasonal unit root while preserving the annual shape.

**Sens slope** (`sens_slope`) — Theil–Sen slope: the median of all pairwise slopes, with a distribution-free interval. Robust to a handful of extreme values.

**Structural break** (`structural_break`) — A date at which the data-generating process changes. Break tests include Chow, Quandt–Andrews, Bai–Perron and CUSUM.

**Unit root** (`unit_root`) — A stochastic trend: shocks never die out and the variance grows with time. Differencing is the usual remedy, but only when the tests agree.

**Zivot–Andrews** (`zivot_andrews`) — A unit-root test that allows one endogenous structural break in intercept, trend or both.

## Decomposition & components

**Amplitude growing** (`amplitude_growing`) — Whether the peak-to-trough seasonal swing widens with the level. It motivates a multiplicative model or a variance-stabilising transform.

**Christiano–Fitzgerald filter** (`christiano_fitzgerald`) — A band-pass filter isolating cyclical frequencies; like HP it produces a cycle rather than a seasonal component.

**Classical decomposition** (`classical_decomposition`) — Moving-average based additive or multiplicative decomposition. Simple, but it cannot handle a changing seasonal shape.

**Cycle** (`cycle`) — A rise and fall with no fixed calendar length — unlike seasonality, you cannot predict when the next turn comes.

**Decomposition** (`decomposition`) — Splitting a series into trend, seasonal, cycle and remainder so each can be measured and described separately.

**F_S (seasonal strength)** (`f_s`) — Hyndman's seasonal-strength measure, computed from an STL fit; reported only when the seasonal model is valid.

**F_T (trend strength)** (`f_t`) — Hyndman's trend-strength measure, 1 minus the variance ratio of remainder to trend-plus-remainder. Capped by the Mann–Kendall verdict.

**Fisher's g-test** (`fisher_g`) — Fisher's exact test for whether the largest periodogram peak is more than spectral noise would produce.

**HP filter** (`hp_filter`) — Hodrick–Prescott filter separating a smooth trend from a cycle. Its second component is a cycle, not a season.

**Kruskal–Wallis** (`kruskal_wallis`) — A distribution-free test of whether seasonal groups differ, used as evidence that a seasonal pattern is real.

**MSTL** (`mstl`) — Multiple STL: decomposes several seasonal periods at once, e.g. daily and weekly cycles in hourly data.

**Multiplicative** (`multiplicative`) — A structure where the seasonal swing scales with the level. It is blocked on non-positive data, exactly like a log transform.

**Periodogram** (`periodogram`) — An estimate of the spectral density. Its peaks reveal cycles, but a tallest peak always exists even in noise.

**Seasonal index** (`seasonal_index`) — The average effect of each season position, in units and as a percentage of the mean.

**STL** (`stl`) — Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess: robust, handles evolving seasonality, and supplies the remainder that trend and adequacy tests use.

**UCM** (`ucm`) — Unobserved-components (structural) model estimated by Kalman filtering; handles missing values natively.

**Variance share** (`variance_share`) — The fraction of total variation attributed to one component. The scorecard ranks components by it.

**X-13ARIMA-SEATS** (`x13`) — X-13ARIMA-SEATS, the official seasonal-adjustment program. Used only when its external binary is installed; otherwise flagged.

## Correlation & model identification

**ACF** (`acf`) — Autocorrelation function across lags. Slow decay suggests non-stationarity; a sharp cutoff suggests an MA order.

**Autocorrelation** (`autocorrelation`) — Correlation between a series and a lagged copy of itself; the basic measure of memory.

**Bartlett bands** (`bartlett_bands`) — Approximate ±1.96/√n confidence bands for a correlogram under white noise.

**Benchmark** (`benchmark`) — A deliberately simple reference model (naive, seasonal naive, mean, drift) that every candidate must beat out of sample.

**CCF** (`ccf`) — Cross-correlation between two series at each lag, used to time-align an exogenous regressor.

**Correlogram** (`correlogram`) — The plotted ACF/PACF with confidence bands and a plain-language pattern classification.

**Information criterion** (`information_criterion`) — AIC, AICc or BIC: fit penalised for parameter count. Comparable only across models with the same differencing and effective sample.

**Leakage** (`leakage`) — Any use of test-period information in a modelling choice. Rolling-origin CV and training-only scaling exist to prevent it.

**Ljung–Box** (`ljung_box`) — A portmanteau test that a whole block of residual autocorrelations is jointly zero, with a lag-adjusted null distribution.

**Model registry** (`model_registry`) — The single table of ModelSpec rows describing every model, its data class, assumptions and required sample size.

**Order hint** (`order_hint`) — A suggested p or q from the ACF/PACF pattern. It is a starting point, always checked by information criteria and CV.

**PACF** (`pacf`) — Partial autocorrelation: correlation at a lag after removing the effect of all shorter lags. A cutoff suggests an AR order.

## Models

**ADIDA** (`adida`) — Aggregate-Disaggregate Intermittent Demand Approach: aggregate to a non-intermittent scale, forecast, then disaggregate.

**ARCH** (`arch`) — Autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity: today's variance depends on past squared shocks.

**ARFIMA** (`arfima`) — Fractionally integrated ARMA for long memory, where the differencing parameter d is non-integer.

**ARIMA** (`arima`) — ARMA applied after d differences, ARIMA(p,d,q); seasonal terms give SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m.

**ARMA** (`arma`) — Autoregressive moving-average model for a stationary series, ARMA(p,q).

**auto-ARIMA** (`auto_arima`) — A bounded order search by AICc with stationarity and invertibility root checks; a deterministic grid is the fallback when pmdarima is absent.

**Croston** (`croston`) — Intermittent-demand method that separately smooths non-zero sizes and inter-arrival intervals.

**Damped trend** (`damped_trend`) — A trend whose slope decays with horizon, preventing absurdly long-run linear extrapolation.

**Drift** (`drift`) — A random walk plus an average drift estimated from first differences.

**EGARCH** (`egarch`) — Exponential GARCH modelling log-variance, so it captures leverage without parameter positivity constraints.

**ETS** (`ets`) — Error-Trend-Seasonal exponential smoothing with an automatic additive/multiplicative, damped grid and a non-positive-data guard.

**FEVD** (`fevd`) — Forecast-error variance decomposition: the share of each variable's forecast uncertainty attributed to each shock.

**Fit failure** (`fit_failure`) — A fit that did not converge is reported as a failure with a reason; it never silently becomes an empty result or a fabricated number.

**Forecast combination** (`forecast_combination`) — Mean, median, information-criterion-weighted or Granger–Ramanathan pooling of component forecasts; requires component forecasts first.

**GARCH** (`garch`) — Generalised ARCH with variance depending on past variances as well as squared shocks; produces both a mean and a variance forecast.

**Gaussian process** (`gaussian_process`) — A non-parametric Bayesian regression over functions, giving a predictive distribution rather than just a point.

**GJR-GARCH** (`gjr_garch`) — Glosten–Jagannathan–Runkle GARCH with an asymmetric response to negative shocks.

**Gradient boosting** (`gradient_boosting`) — LightGBM/XGBoost boosted trees with a mandatory model card stating features, tuning and benchmark comparison.

**Granger causality** (`granger_causality`) — A predictive, not causal, test: X Granger-causes Y if lags of X improve a forecast of Y.

**Hawkes process** (`hawkes`) — A self-exciting point process where each event raises the short-term intensity of further events.

**Holt–Winters** (`holt_winters`) — Classical exponential smoothing with explicit level, trend and seasonal updating equations.

**Hurdle** (`hurdle`) — A two-part model where a binary process decides whether any event occurs, then a truncated count model gives the size.

**INAR(1)** (`inar`) — Integer-valued autoregression using binomial thinning; flagged as advanced in the registry.

**INGARCH** (`ingarch`) — Integer-valued GARCH: a count model whose conditional mean follows a GARCH-like recursion.

**IRF** (`irf`) — Impulse-response function: the path of a system after a one-unit shock, with bootstrap bands.

**Johansen test** (`johansen`) — A likelihood-based test for the number of cointegrating relationships in a system.

**Leverage effect** (`leverage_effect`) — The tendency of negative returns to raise future volatility more than positive returns of the same size.

**Markov switching** (`markov_switching`) — A model whose parameters switch between regimes according to a latent Markov chain.

**Mean model** (`mean_model`) — Forecast equals the historical mean; the baseline for a stationary, structureless series.

**Model card** (`model_card`) — A short record of a fitted model's features, assumptions, training window and out-of-sample benchmark, required for every ML entrant.

**Naive** (`naive`) — Forecast equals the last observed value. The mandatory baseline; MASE is scaled by its in-sample error.

**Negative binomial** (`negative_binomial`) — NB2 count model allowing variance to exceed the mean, compared to Poisson by a likelihood-ratio test and AIC.

**NNAR** (`nna`) — Neural-network autoregression using lagged values as features.

**Poisson model** (`poisson_model`) — A count model with a log link and time-varying intensity; requires an overdispersion pre-check.

**Random forest** (`random_forest`) — An ensemble of decision trees on leakage-safe lag features, always benchmarked against ETS/ARIMA even when it loses.

**Renewal process** (`renewal_process`) — A model of event timestamps based on the distribution of inter-arrival times.

**Root check** (`root_check`) — Verification that AR and MA polynomials have roots outside the unit circle, i.e. the fit is stationary and invertible.

**SARIMAX / ARIMAX** (`sarimax`) — SARIMA with exogenous regressors, used for interventions (pulse/step dummies) and future scenario paths.

**SBA** (`sba`) — Syntetos–Boylan approximation, a bias-corrected variant of Croston.

**Seasonal naive** (`seasonal_naive`) — Forecast equals the value one season ago. The correct baseline for strongly seasonal series.

**SETAR** (`setar`) — Self-exciting threshold autoregression: different AR regimes depending on a lagged value crossing a threshold.

**SVR** (`svr`) — Support-vector regression on lag features with an explicit kernel and scaling.

**Theta method** (`theta`) — The Theta method, equivalent to a drifted SES decomposition; θ controls how much the curvature is retained.

**TSB** (`tsb`) — Teunter–Syntetos–Babai method that updates the occurrence probability every period, including zero-demand periods.

**VAR** (`var`) — Vector autoregression: every variable is regressed on lags of itself and of the others.

**VECM** (`vecm`) — Vector error-correction model for cointegrated series, with a spurious-regression guard.

**Zero inflated** (`zero_inflated`) — A two-part model for excess zeros: one process generates structural zeros, another the counts.

## Forecasting

**Analytic interval** (`analytic_interval`) — An interval from a closed-form forecast variance under a Gaussian assumption.

**Back transformation** (`back_transformation`) — Returning a forecast to the original scale after a log/Box–Cox transform, with a bias adjustment because E[exp X] ≠ exp(E[X]).

**Calibration** (`calibration`) — Whether empirical coverage matches nominal coverage across interval levels.

**Discrete predictive distribution** (`discrete_predictive_distribution`) — A full probability mass function over future counts, needed for CRPS and PIT on count or intermittent data.

**Fan chart** (`fan_chart`) — A plot of several nested prediction intervals with deepening shades, so uncertainty widening with horizon is visible.

**Forecast** (`forecast`) — A predictive distribution for future observations, not just a single number. The app attaches coverage and a residual-adequacy verdict.

**Hierarchical reconciliation** (`hierarchical_reconciliation`) — Adjusting forecasts at different aggregation levels so they add up consistently.

**Horizon** (`horizon`) — How many steps ahead are predicted. The app flags horizons beyond roughly one fifth of the training length.

**Horizon advisor** (`horizon_advisor`) — Guidance on a defensible horizon given sample length, frequency and seasonal period.

**Point forecast** (`point_forecast`) — A single central value (mean or median) for each future step.

**Prediction interval** (`prediction_interval`) — An interval intended to contain the future observation with a stated nominal coverage and a stated construction method.

**Scenario** (`scenario`) — A user-supplied future path for an exogenous regressor, e.g. a marketing-spend plan.

**Sharpness** (`sharpness`) — How narrow a predictive distribution is. Valued only subject to calibration — a narrow but dishonest interval is worse.

**Simulation interval** (`simulation_interval`) — An interval from quantiles of seeded simulated paths, used when no analytic variance exists.

## Evaluation

**Clark–West** (`clark_west`) — A small-sample correction to the Diebold–Mariano comparison for nested models.

**CRPS** (`crps`) — Continuous Ranked Probability Score: a proper score for a whole predictive distribution, rewarding accuracy and honest uncertainty (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007).

**Diebold–Mariano** (`diebold_mariano`) — A test of whether two forecasts have equal expected loss, with HAC-corrected variance for multi-step errors.

**Dunn–Smyth residuals** (`dunn_smyth`) — Dunn–Smyth residuals for count models, a randomised normal residual used in the discrete diagnostic battery.

**Fold** (`fold`) — One train/test split in rolling-origin CV; the app reports fold-level accuracy, not just the average.

**IC comparability guard** (`ic_comparable`) — The guard that refuses AIC/BIC comparisons across different differencing orders or effective sample sizes.

**KS test** (`ks_test`) — Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of PIT uniformity against the uniform distribution.

**Log score** (`log_score`) — Minus the log predictive density at the observation. Proper but sensitive to tails; the continuous-case caveat is stated.

**MAE** (`mae`) — Mean absolute error. Robust, in the units of the series, and the primary point error on zero-heavy data.

**MAPE** (`mape`) — Mean absolute percentage error. Banned on intermittent and zero-heavy data because it is undefined or explodes near zero.

**MASE** (`mase`) — Mean Absolute Scaled Error: MAE divided by the in-sample naive error. Below 1 beats 'tomorrow equals today'; 0 for a perfect forecast, 1 for the naive one.

**Mase by horizon** (`mase_by_horizon`) — MASE computed separately at each forecast step, revealing whether a model degrades gracefully with horizon.

**Metric policy** (`metric_policy`) — The rule engine that bans MAPE on zero-heavy data, switches to CRPS when a probabilistic forecast exists, and always prints a reason.

**Out of sample** (`out_of_sample`) — Computed only on observations held out of fitting. In-sample fit is never reported as forecast accuracy.

**PI coverage** (`pi_coverage`) — Empirical fraction of observations inside an interval, compared with its nominal coverage.

**Pinball loss** (`pinball_loss`) — Quantile (check) loss averaged over quantile levels; the proper score behind quantile forecasts.

**PIT** (`pit`) — Probability Integral Transform: if the forecast distribution is honest these values are uniform; systematic shapes reveal over- or under-confidence.

**Relative metric** (`relative_metric`) — Any error divided by a benchmark error or a training-only scale. §6.4 forbids computing one before the naive benchmark is fitted.

**RMSE** (`rmse`) — Root mean squared error; penalises large misses more than MAE.

**RMSSE** (`rmsse`) — Root Mean Squared Scaled Error, the RMSE analogue of MASE, using the same training-only denominator.

**Rolling origin cv** (`rolling_origin_cv`) — Time-ordered cross-validation that expands the training window and always keeps the test block in the future.

**RQR** (`rqr`) — Randomised Quantile Residuals: normal-like residuals for discrete or non-normal models, obtained by randomising within predictive probabilities.

**sMAPE** (`smape`) — Symmetric absolute percentage error, capped at 200%; shown only for comparability, never as a genuine percentage error.

**Winkler score** (`winkler_score`) — Interval score penalising both width and misses outside a prediction interval.

## Preprocessing

**Advisor** (`advisor`) — A rule engine that ranks recommendations from computed statistics and attaches the evidence, confidence and a 'what if ignored' note.

**Aggregation** (`aggregation`) — Summing or averaging to a coarser frequency, e.g. daily to weekly, to remove an intermittent zero problem.

**Box cox** (`box_cox`) — A power transform indexed by λ; λ=0 is a log, λ=1 means no transform. Its confidence interval is printed with the recommendation.

**Caveat** (`caveat`) — A qualification that travels with downstream results so a forecast or report never hides a known limitation.

**Imputation** (`imputation`) — Filling missing values with an explicit, previewable rule (seasonal, Kalman) rather than a silent default.

**Log transform** (`log_transform`) — Taking logarithms to stabilise a variance that grows with the level. Blocked on non-positive values; Yeo–Johnson is used instead.

**Outlier treatment** (`outlier_treatment`) — Flagging or replacing unusual observations. The app prefers flagging (and intervention dummies) to deleting rows.

**Preview** (`preview`) — Running the exact same operation on a copy of the series before committing, so what the user sees is what happens.

**Readiness gate** (`readiness_gate`) — The S8 checklist of blockers and caveats that must be resolved before model suggestion is allowed.

**Redo** (`redo`) — Re-applying the most recently undone treatment; a new treatment clears the redo history, exactly like an editor.

**Series version** (`series_version`) — A counter bumped whenever the series changes. Results record the version they describe so stale panels can be marked.

**Smoothing** (`smoothing`) — Averaging neighbouring values to reduce measurement noise; it changes the series and therefore invalidates downstream results.

**Stale** (`stale`) — A completed stage whose inputs have since changed. The UI says 'Needs re-running' instead of reusing an obsolete number.

**Transform** (`transform`) — A monotone rescaling of the values, e.g. log, square root, Box–Cox or Yeo–Johnson.

**Undo** (`undo`) — Stepping back one treatment by replaying the remaining chain from the untouched original series.

**Yeojohnson** (`yeojohnson`) — A power transform defined for zero and negative values too, behaving like a log on positive values.

## Reporting & reproducibility

**Alt text** (`alt_text`) — A screen-reader description of a figure or table that summarises the actual values, not just 'chart'.

**Analysis digest** (`analysis_digest`) — The compact, number-only summary of computed results that grounds every AI answer; no raw values are included by default.

**Background job** (`background_job`) — Heavy work (CV grids, ML fits, demo replays) executed off the request thread with progress, per-step timings and cancel.

**Caption** (`caption`) — A one-sentence description of a figure or table, generated from the computed values, not hand-written.

**.chronos archive** (`chronos_archive`) — A .chronos session export containing the pipeline state and results, so a study can be reloaded exactly.

**Coverage** (`coverage`) — The share of source lines executed by the test suite. §5.15 requires at least 80% on ts/.

**Data behind** (`data_behind`) — The exact numbers behind any plot or table, downloadable as XLSX/CSV so a figure is never the only record.

**Delete session** (`delete_session`) — A button that hard-deletes the session from server memory immediately.

**Demo mode** (`demo_mode`) — One click that replays a complete seed study through S0–S15 with progress and cancel, producing a real explorable analysis.

**DPI** (`dpi`) — Dots per inch; publication figures are exported at 300 dpi plus vector SVG and PDF.

**Golden file** (`golden_file`) — A stored, reviewed reference output that a test compares against, so an unintended statistical change fails the build.

**Library versions** (`library_versions`) — The recorded versions of numpy/pandas/statsmodels/scikit-learn used for a study, so a result can be reproduced later.

**Methods document** (`methods_document`) — METHODS.md: exactly which test, implementation and assumption is used for every reported number — the document a thesis committee reads.

**Offline mode** (`offline_mode`) — The deterministic narrative assistant that needs no API key; removing the AI layer leaves a fully functional app.

**One-file HTML** (`one_file_html`) — A self-contained report with embedded figures and no external CSS, scripts or fonts, so it works offline.

**Payload preview** (`payload_preview`) — A review of exactly what would be sent to the AI service before the first live request; data values are off by default.

**Privacy note** (`privacy_note`) — A plain-English statement of what is stored, what is sent to an AI service, and what is exported only on request.

**Report bundle** (`report_bundle`) — A ZIP containing every requested format plus a manifest; builder failures are listed in errors.txt rather than hidden.

**Reproducible snippet** (`reproducible_snippet`) — A Python or R script exported with the analysis that regenerates the numbers from the raw data; it must parse as valid source.

**Scorecard** (`scorecard`) — Ten weighted completeness checks with exact result links and the panel to visit for each outstanding item.

**Seed data** (`seed_data`) — The bundled example datasets shipped with the image so a new user needs no upload and the build needs no network.

**Session ttl** (`session_ttl`) — The in-memory lifetime of a session. There is no server-side database and no persistence of user data beyond this window.

**Verdict** (`verdict`) — The exact manuscript-readiness sentence: ready, nearly ready with two outstanding items, or not yet with blockers.

## Product & accessibility

**ARIA live region** (`aria_live`) — A region that announces asynchronous changes (progress, errors, toasts) without moving keyboard focus.

**Colorblind safe** (`colorblind_safe`) — A palette distinguishable under the common colour-vision deficiencies; every status also carries text and an icon.

**Error library** (`error_library`) — Plain-English error messages with a code, a fix and a technical detail, so a failure is never a dead end.

**Focus visible** (`focus_visible`) — A clear keyboard focus ring that appears for keyboard users but not on mouse clicks.

**Guided tour** (`guided_tour`) — A step-by-step walkthrough of a worked analysis with next, back and skip controls.

**No color only** (`no_color_only`) — The rule that colour never carries meaning by itself — verdicts add words, icons and shapes.

**Plain language mode** (`plain_language_mode`) — A toggle that suppresses the technical layer of a result card and keeps the plain-English reading.

**Reduced motion** (`reduced_motion`) — Respecting the operating-system 'prefers-reduced-motion' setting by suppressing transitions and animations.

**Ribbon** (`ribbon`) — The JASP-style command bar. It implements the WAI-ARIA toolbar pattern: one tab stop, arrow keys between commands, Home/End to jump.

**Screen reader** (`screen_reader`) — Assistive technology that reads the accessible name and description of each control, figure and table.

**Simplify view** (`simplify_view`) — A mode that hides all but the eight essential panels so a beginner is not confronted with the full 16-stage ribbon.

**Stepper** (`stepper`) — The pipeline navigation bar; completed steps can be revisited, and gated steps explain which earlier step is missing.

**Table caption** (`table_caption`) — A visible title on every data table, paired with a value summary for screen readers.

**Tooltip** (`tooltip`) — A short definition shown on hover and on keyboard focus; the glossary supplies 120+ of them and never relies on colour alone.

**WCAG 2.1 AA** (`wcag`) — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 AA: the target standard for contrast, keyboard operation and screen-reader labels.
